title: Physics Midterm — Quick Recall (Clear Answer Types)
subject: Physics
description: 179 short-answer flashcards clearly labeled FORMULA, DEFINITION, RULE, VALUE, TERM, UNIT, CONVERSION, etc. No worked math problems.

cards.front: RULE • For measured addition (+): round using what?
cards.explanation: In addition, the least precise decimal place among the measurements determines the answer's rounding place.

cards.front: RULE • For measured subtraction (−): round using what?
cards.explanation: In subtraction, round the final result to the fewest decimal places present in the measured inputs.

cards.front: RULE • For measured multiplication (×): round using what?
cards.explanation: For multiplication, the input with the fewest significant digits determines how many digits remain in the result.

cards.front: RULE • For measured division (÷): round using what?
cards.explanation: For division, the input with the fewest significant digits limits the number of significant digits in the result.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What are significant figures?
cards.explanation: Significant figures communicate measurement precision: the reliable digits and the final estimated digit.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What are decimal places?
cards.explanation: Decimal places are digits to the right of the decimal point; they control precision when adding or subtracting measurements.

cards.front: YES / NO • Do nonzero digits count as significant?
cards.explanation: All digits from 1 through 9 are significant because they carry measured information.

cards.front: YES / NO • Do leading zeros count as significant?
cards.explanation: Zeros before the first nonzero digit only locate the decimal point; they do not represent measured precision.

cards.front: YES / NO • Do zeros between nonzero digits count?
cards.explanation: Zeros between nonzero digits are significant because they are part of the measured value.

cards.front: YES / NO • Do trailing zeros after a decimal count?
cards.explanation: Trailing zeros after a decimal can indicate measured precision, so they count as significant.

cards.front: TERM • Name the NOTATION used to show significant trailing zeros clearly.
cards.explanation: Scientific notation makes precision explicit: 4.0 × 10³ has two significant figures, whereas 4 × 10³ has one.

cards.front: RULE • Do exact counted quantities limit significant figures?
cards.explanation: An exact count or defined conversion has no measurement uncertainty, so it does not limit significant figures.

cards.front: RULE • Should you round intermediate calculations early?
cards.explanation: Keep extra calculator digits in intermediate steps; rounding too soon may change the final answer.

cards.front: RULE • State the RULE for the sequence of mixed calculations.
cards.explanation: Follow the normal order of operations, but apply the relevant precision rule to each operation and round only at the end.

cards.front: RULE • Name the PRECISION RULE for + and −.
cards.explanation: Addition and subtraction are limited by the least precise decimal place, not by the smallest significant-figure count.

cards.front: RULE • Name the PRECISION RULE for × and ÷.
cards.explanation: Multiplication and division are limited by the fewest significant figures, not by the decimal-place count.

cards.front: TERM • Which zero type never counts as significant?
cards.explanation: Leading zeros before the first nonzero digit do not contribute to the precision of a measurement.

cards.front: TERM • Which zeros always count between nonzero digits?
cards.explanation: Captive zeros, lying between nonzero digits, always count as significant figures.

cards.front: PURPOSE • What is dimensional analysis used for?
cards.explanation: Dimensional analysis changes units using equivalent fractions without changing the physical quantity.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a conversion factor?
cards.explanation: A conversion factor, such as 100 cm / 1 m, equals one because numerator and denominator represent the same length.

cards.front: RESULT • What happens to unwanted units in dimensional analysis?
cards.explanation: Place the unwanted unit opposite itself in conversion fractions so it cancels algebraically.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 kilometer equals how many meters?
cards.explanation: The prefix kilo- means 1,000; therefore 1 km is exactly 1,000 meters.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 meter equals how many centimeters?
cards.explanation: The prefix centi- means one hundredth; 100 centimeters make exactly one meter.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 kilogram equals how many grams?
cards.explanation: A kilogram contains exactly 1,000 grams by the metric prefix definition.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 gram equals how many milligrams?
cards.explanation: A gram contains exactly 1,000 milligrams; milli- means one thousandth.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 hour equals how many minutes?
cards.explanation: One hour consists of 60 minutes; this is an exact time relationship.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 hour equals how many seconds?
cards.explanation: One hour contains 60 × 60 = 3,600 seconds; this is an exact conversion.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 minute equals how many seconds?
cards.explanation: One minute is exactly 60 seconds, so this conversion does not limit significant figures.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 foot equals how many inches?
cards.explanation: One foot is defined as exactly 12 inches.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 mile equals how many feet?
cards.explanation: One mile is defined as exactly 5,280 feet.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 inch equals how many centimeters?
cards.explanation: The international inch is defined as exactly 2.54 centimeters.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 liter equals how many cubic centimeters?
cards.explanation: A liter is exactly 1,000 cubic centimeters; it is a volume, not an area.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 cubic meter equals how many liters?
cards.explanation: One cubic meter contains 1,000 liters because one liter is 0.001 cubic meter.

cards.front: EXACT CONVERSION • 1 carat equals how many grams?
cards.explanation: The guide uses 1 carat = 0.2 grams as a given conversion for the diamond problem.

cards.front: FORMULA • State the FORMULA for average speed.
cards.explanation: Average speed divides distance traveled by elapsed time; use matching units.

cards.front: FORMULA • State the FORMULA for density.
cards.explanation: Density divides mass by volume, typically kilograms per cubic meter or grams per cubic centimeter.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does the symbol ρ (rho) mean?
cards.explanation: The Greek letter rho (ρ) is commonly used for mass density.

cards.front: UNIT • What is the SI unit of speed?
cards.explanation: Meters per second measure how much distance is traveled each second.

cards.front: UNIT • What is the SI unit of acceleration?
cards.explanation: Meters per second squared measure how much velocity changes each second.

cards.front: UNIT • What is a common density unit?
cards.explanation: Kilograms per cubic meter expresses mass contained in a unit volume.

cards.front: EXPONENT • What exponent applies to an area conversion?
cards.explanation: Area is two-dimensional, so square the whole length conversion factor.

cards.front: EXPONENT • What exponent applies to a volume conversion?
cards.explanation: Volume is three-dimensional, so cube the whole length conversion factor.

cards.front: NUMBER • An echo travels how many times the one-way distance?
cards.explanation: An echo travels to the reflecting surface and back; total travel distance is twice the one-way distance.

cards.front: APPROX. VALUE • Speed of sound in air at 20°C?
cards.explanation: About 343 m/s describes sound moving through air near 20 °C, not a universal fixed constant.

cards.front: YES / NO • Is sound speed constant at every temperature?
cards.explanation: Air temperature affects sound speed; use a value supplied by the problem or state an approximation.

cards.front: UNIT • What units measure area?
cards.explanation: Area is length multiplied by length, producing units such as m² or cm².

cards.front: UNIT • What units measure volume?
cards.explanation: Volume uses three length dimensions, producing units such as m³ or cm³.

cards.front: ABBREVIATION • Speed in miles per hour is abbreviated how?
cards.explanation: Miles per hour abbreviates as mph; speed is distance divided by time.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a scalar?
cards.explanation: A scalar has size only; it has no specified direction, unlike velocity or displacement.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a vector?
cards.explanation: A vector has both magnitude and direction, often drawn as an arrow.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is displacement?
cards.explanation: Displacement points from starting position to ending position; it differs from total path length.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is vector magnitude?
cards.explanation: A vector's magnitude is its nonnegative size, regardless of direction.

cards.front: AXIS • Which axis is horizontal?
cards.explanation: The horizontal component of a vector is conventionally plotted on the x-axis.

cards.front: AXIS • Which axis is vertical?
cards.explanation: The vertical component of a vector is conventionally plotted on the y-axis.

cards.front: SIGN • What sign represents east on the x-axis?
cards.explanation: With east chosen positive, an eastward component has a positive x-value.

cards.front: SIGN • What sign represents west on the x-axis?
cards.explanation: With east positive, a westward component has a negative x-value.

cards.front: SIGN • What sign represents north on the y-axis?
cards.explanation: With north chosen positive, a northward component has a positive y-value.

cards.front: SIGN • What sign represents south on the y-axis?
cards.explanation: With north positive, a southward component has a negative y-value.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a resultant vector?
cards.explanation: The resultant combines the individual vectors into one net vector.

cards.front: THEOREM NAME • Resultant magnitude from perpendicular components: which theorem?
cards.explanation: Perpendicular components form a right triangle; the Pythagorean theorem gives the resultant magnitude.

cards.front: FORMULA • Magnitude from perpendicular x and y components.
cards.explanation: This magnitude formula works when x and y are perpendicular components with the same units.

cards.front: FORMULA • X-component when θ is measured from +x.
cards.explanation: When θ is measured from the positive x-axis, the horizontal component is the magnitude times cosine.

cards.front: FORMULA • Y-component when θ is measured from +x.
cards.explanation: When θ is measured from the positive x-axis, the vertical component is the magnitude times sine.

cards.front: FORMULA • Vector direction from x and y components.
cards.explanation: The two-argument atan2 function uses both signed components, so it can determine the correct quadrant.

cards.front: TRIG RATIO • Give the TRIG RATIO for sine (SOH).
cards.explanation: SOH means sine equals opposite divided by hypotenuse, measured relative to the selected angle.

cards.front: TRIG RATIO • Give the TRIG RATIO for cosine (CAH).
cards.explanation: CAH means cosine equals adjacent divided by hypotenuse, measured relative to the selected angle.

cards.front: TRIG RATIO • Give the TRIG RATIO for tangent (TOA).
cards.explanation: TOA means tangent equals opposite divided by adjacent, measured relative to the selected angle.

cards.front: FUNCTION NAME • Which trig function uses opposite and adjacent?
cards.explanation: Use tangent when the opposite and adjacent sides are the relevant sides.

cards.front: FUNCTION NAME • Which trig function uses opposite and hypotenuse?
cards.explanation: Use sine when the opposite side and hypotenuse are the relevant sides.

cards.front: FUNCTION NAME • Which trig function uses adjacent and hypotenuse?
cards.explanation: Use cosine when the adjacent side and hypotenuse are the relevant sides.

cards.front: FUNCTION NAME • Which function finds an angle from a trig ratio?
cards.explanation: Use inverse sine, cosine, or tangent to recover an angle from a side ratio.

cards.front: CALCULATOR MODE • What calculator mode is used for degree angles?
cards.explanation: Set the calculator to degrees when the given angles and required answers are in degrees.

cards.front: DEFINITION • Define the hypotenuse of a RIGHT TRIANGLE.
cards.explanation: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse lies opposite the 90° angle and is the longest side.

cards.front: ANGLE VALUE • What angle defines a right triangle?
cards.explanation: A right triangle has one 90° angle, allowing the Pythagorean theorem and SOHCAHTOA.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is kinematics?
cards.explanation: Kinematics describes motion—position, velocity, and acceleration—without focusing on the forces causing it.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is distance?
cards.explanation: Distance measures the full length of a traveled path, without direction.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is velocity?
cards.explanation: Velocity combines speed with a direction, so it is a vector.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is acceleration?
cards.explanation: Acceleration describes the rate at which velocity changes with time; its SI unit is m/s².

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does t represent?
cards.explanation: The variable t is elapsed time, usually measured in seconds.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does vᵢ represent?
cards.explanation: Initial velocity is the velocity at the beginning of the interval under study.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does v𝒇 represent?
cards.explanation: Final velocity is the velocity at the end of that interval.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does Δx represent?
cards.explanation: Δx is change in horizontal position, or final x minus initial x.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does Δy represent?
cards.explanation: Δy is change in vertical position, or final y minus initial y.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does g represent?
cards.explanation: The symbol g describes the acceleration caused by gravity near Earth's surface.

cards.front: STANDARD VALUE • Magnitude of g near Earth?
cards.explanation: Near Earth's surface, g is commonly approximated as 9.8 m/s² in the downward direction.

cards.front: DIRECTION • Direction of gravity near Earth?
cards.explanation: Gravity points toward Earth; if upward is positive, vertical acceleration is −g.

cards.front: YES / NO • Is g = 9.8 m/s² exact everywhere?
cards.explanation: Gravity varies slightly with location and altitude; 9.8 m/s² is a standard approximation.

cards.front: VALUE • Starting from rest: initial velocity?
cards.explanation: Starting from rest means initial speed is zero, before motion begins.

cards.front: VALUE • Dropped object: initial vertical velocity?
cards.explanation: For a dropped object, initial vertical velocity is zero if it is released without a push.

cards.front: VALUE • Horizontally launched object: initial vertical velocity?
cards.explanation: A horizontal launch has no initial vertical velocity, although gravity immediately accelerates it downward.

cards.front: VALUE • At the top of projectile flight: vertical velocity?
cards.explanation: At the highest point, vertical velocity is momentarily zero; horizontal velocity may remain nonzero.

cards.front: VALUE • Without air drag: horizontal acceleration?
cards.explanation: With air resistance neglected, no horizontal force changes horizontal velocity, so ax = 0.

cards.front: BEHAVIOR • Without air drag: horizontal velocity?
cards.explanation: Without air resistance, horizontal velocity remains constant throughout projectile flight.

cards.front: AXIS • For projectile motion, which axis has gravitational acceleration?
cards.explanation: Gravity acts vertically, so the projectile's gravitational acceleration is along the y-axis.

cards.front: SHARED QUANTITY • Which quantity is shared by horizontal and vertical motion?
cards.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motion have the same elapsed flight time even though their velocities differ.

cards.front: FORMULA • Final velocity using vᵢ, a, and t (constant a).
cards.explanation: This constant-acceleration equation finds final velocity from initial velocity, acceleration, and elapsed time.

cards.front: FORMULA • Displacement using vᵢ, a, and t (constant a).
cards.explanation: This equation finds displacement from initial velocity, acceleration, and time when acceleration stays constant.

cards.front: FORMULA • Give the FORMULA relating v𝒇, vᵢ, a, and Δx (no time).
cards.explanation: Use the squared-velocity relation when time is absent and acceleration is constant.

cards.front: FORMULA • Fall distance from rest (constant g).
cards.explanation: An object dropped from rest falls distance h = ½gt² if air drag is negligible and g is constant.

cards.front: FORMULA • Fall time from rest, given height h.
cards.explanation: Rearrange h = ½gt² to find drop time; choose the nonnegative square root.

cards.front: FORMULA • Launch horizontal velocity from v₀ and θ.
cards.explanation: For a launch angle from horizontal, multiply launch speed by cosine to get horizontal velocity.

cards.front: FORMULA • Launch vertical velocity from v₀ and θ.
cards.explanation: For a launch angle from horizontal, multiply launch speed by sine to get vertical velocity.

cards.front: FORMULA • Vertical velocity during a projectile (up = +).
cards.explanation: With upward positive, subtract gt from initial vertical velocity to find vertical velocity later.

cards.front: FORMULA • Horizontal displacement with no air drag.
cards.explanation: With no horizontal acceleration, horizontal displacement equals horizontal velocity times time.

cards.front: FORMULA • Vertical displacement of a projectile (up = +).
cards.explanation: With upward positive and negligible drag, vertical displacement equals v₀yt − ½gt².

cards.front: FORMULA • Flight time if launch and landing heights match.
cards.explanation: Flight time equals 2v₀y/g only if the projectile lands at the height from which it launched.

cards.front: FORMULA • Speed from horizontal and vertical velocities.
cards.explanation: Use the Pythagorean theorem on perpendicular velocity components to find total speed.

cards.front: YES / NO • Can equal-height flight-time formula apply to cliff landings?
cards.explanation: A cliff landing has a different final height, so the equal-height shortcut for flight time is invalid.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a force?
cards.explanation: Force is a push or pull that may change an object's velocity or shape.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is net force?
cards.explanation: Net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on one object.

cards.front: UNIT • SI unit of force?
cards.explanation: The SI force unit is the newton, symbol N.

cards.front: EXACT UNIT RELATION • one newton equals?
cards.explanation: A newton is defined as 1 kg·m/s², linking force to mass and acceleration.

cards.front: FORMULA • Newton’s SECOND LAW?
cards.explanation: Newton's second law says net force equals mass times acceleration.

cards.front: FORMULA • Net force from mass and acceleration.
cards.explanation: Multiply mass by acceleration to calculate the net force on an object.

cards.front: FORMULA • Acceleration from net force and mass.
cards.explanation: Divide net force by mass to calculate acceleration, with consistent SI units.

cards.front: UNIT • What is mass measured in?
cards.explanation: Mass measures resistance to acceleration and is expressed in kilograms.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is weight?
cards.explanation: Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object's mass, not the mass itself.

cards.front: FORMULA • Weight near Earth.
cards.explanation: Near Earth, weight equals mass times gravitational acceleration; the result is in newtons.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does N mean as a force variable?
cards.explanation: In a force diagram, N often denotes normal force; after a number, N denotes the newton unit.

cards.front: DIRECTION • Direction of normal force?
cards.explanation: A surface's normal force pushes perpendicular to that surface.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is tension?
cards.explanation: Tension is the pulling force transmitted by a rope or string.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is friction?
cards.explanation: Friction resists relative sliding, or the tendency to slide, between contacting surfaces.

cards.front: SYMBOL • What does μₖ represent?
cards.explanation: The kinetic friction coefficient μk is a property of the contacting surfaces while sliding.

cards.front: YES / NO • Does μₖ have units?
cards.explanation: A friction coefficient is a ratio of forces, so it has no units.

cards.front: FORMULA • Kinetic friction while sliding.
cards.explanation: Kinetic friction equals μk times normal force when the surfaces are sliding.

cards.front: DIRECTION • Direction of kinetic friction?
cards.explanation: Kinetic friction opposes the direction of relative sliding between surfaces.

cards.front: VALUE • At rest: net force?
cards.explanation: At rest with no acceleration, all forces must balance to a zero net force.

cards.front: VALUE • At constant velocity: net force?
cards.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration; Newton's second law then gives zero net force.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is equilibrium?
cards.explanation: Mechanical equilibrium means the vector sum of forces is zero.

cards.front: FORMULA • Gravity PARALLEL to a ramp.
cards.explanation: On a ramp, the component of gravity down the slope is mg sinθ.

cards.front: FORMULA • Gravity PERPENDICULAR to a ramp.
cards.explanation: On a ramp, the component of gravity pressing into the surface is mg cosθ.

cards.front: FORMULA • Normal force on a simple ramp (no extra forces).
cards.explanation: On a simple incline with no other perpendicular forces, the normal force is mg cosθ.

cards.front: FORMULA • Horizontal applied-force component at θ.
cards.explanation: For an applied force at θ above horizontal, the horizontal component uses cosine.

cards.front: FORMULA • Vertical applied-force component at θ.
cards.explanation: For an applied force at θ above horizontal, the vertical component uses sine.

cards.front: EFFECT • Angled upward pull changes normal force how?
cards.explanation: An upward pull partly lifts the object, reducing the normal force and usually kinetic friction.

cards.front: EFFECT • Angled downward push changes normal force how?
cards.explanation: A downward angled push presses the object harder into the surface, increasing normal force.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is an Atwood machine?
cards.explanation: An ideal Atwood machine has two hanging masses connected by a light rope over a frictionless pulley.

cards.front: WHICH MASS • Ideal Atwood pulley: which mass descends?
cards.explanation: In an ideal Atwood machine, the heavier mass accelerates downward and the lighter one upward.

cards.front: FORMULA • Ideal Atwood-machine acceleration.
cards.explanation: The ideal Atwood formula assumes two hanging masses, negligible pulley friction, and a massless rope.

cards.front: PROPERTY • In an ideal rope, how does tension vary?
cards.explanation: Tension is constant along an ideal massless rope passing over a frictionless pulley.

cards.front: PROPERTY • In an ideal rope, both masses have what acceleration size?
cards.explanation: A taut, inextensible rope makes the linked masses accelerate with equal magnitudes.

cards.front: FORCE NAME • Elevator scale measures which force?
cards.explanation: A scale reads the normal force it exerts on the person, known as apparent weight.

cards.front: EFFECT • Elevator accelerating upward: apparent weight?
cards.explanation: Upward acceleration requires a normal force greater than weight, so the scale reads higher.

cards.front: EFFECT • Elevator accelerating downward: apparent weight?
cards.explanation: Downward acceleration requires a normal force less than weight, so the scale reads lower.

cards.front: EFFECT • Elevator moving at constant speed: apparent weight?
cards.explanation: At constant velocity, acceleration is zero, so normal force equals mg in a vertical elevator.

cards.front: FORMULA • Elevator net force (up positive).
cards.explanation: With upward positive, normal force minus weight equals mass times vertical acceleration.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What does a free-body diagram show?
cards.explanation: A free-body diagram shows only forces acting on the selected object, drawn as arrows.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is electric current?
cards.explanation: Electric current measures how much electric charge passes a point each second.

cards.front: SYMBOL • Symbol for current?
cards.explanation: Capital I is the standard symbol for electric current.

cards.front: UNIT • Unit of current?
cards.explanation: An ampere is the SI unit of electric current, equal to one coulomb per second.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is voltage?
cards.explanation: Voltage measures the electric potential difference between two points.

cards.front: SYMBOL • Symbol for voltage?
cards.explanation: Capital V commonly represents voltage in elementary circuit formulas.

cards.front: UNIT • Unit of voltage?
cards.explanation: A volt is the SI unit of electric potential difference.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is electrical resistance?
cards.explanation: Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes electric current.

cards.front: SYMBOL • Symbol for resistance?
cards.explanation: Capital R represents resistance in Ohm's law.

cards.front: UNIT • Unit of resistance?
cards.explanation: An ohm, symbol Ω, is the SI unit of electrical resistance.

cards.front: EXACT UNIT RELATION • State the EXACT UNIT RELATION for 1 ohm (Ω).
cards.explanation: One ohm equals one volt per ampere, following R = V/I.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is electrical power?
cards.explanation: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred or used.

cards.front: SYMBOL • Symbol for electrical power?
cards.explanation: Capital P represents electrical power in circuit equations.

cards.front: UNIT • Unit of electrical power?
cards.explanation: A watt is the SI unit of power, equal to one joule per second.

cards.front: FORMULA • Ohm’s Law?
cards.explanation: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance as V = IR.

cards.front: FORMULA • Current from voltage and resistance.
cards.explanation: Divide voltage by resistance to find current in an ohmic resistor.

cards.front: FORMULA • Resistance from voltage and current.
cards.explanation: Divide voltage by current to find resistance for an ohmic resistor.

cards.front: FORMULA • Voltage from current and resistance.
cards.explanation: Multiply current by resistance to find voltage using Ohm's law.

cards.front: FORMULA • Power from current and voltage.
cards.explanation: Multiply voltage by current to find electrical power.

cards.front: FORMULA • Current from power and voltage.
cards.explanation: Divide electrical power by voltage to find current, provided voltage is nonzero.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a series circuit?
cards.explanation: In series, components form one continuous current path.

cards.front: PROPERTY • What stays equal in series resistors?
cards.explanation: Because only one path exists, the same current flows through each series component.

cards.front: PROPERTY • What adds across series resistors?
cards.explanation: The individual voltage drops in a series loop add up to the source voltage.

cards.front: FORMULA • Equivalent resistance in series.
cards.explanation: In series, resistances add directly to find their equivalent resistance.

cards.front: EFFECT • If one series bulb burns out, what happens?
cards.explanation: A break anywhere in a simple series circuit interrupts the only current path.

cards.front: DEFINITION • What is a parallel circuit?
cards.explanation: Parallel components occupy separate branches across the same two nodes.

cards.front: PROPERTY • What stays equal across parallel branches?
cards.explanation: Each parallel branch is connected across the same two nodes, so branch voltages match.

cards.front: PROPERTY • What adds at a parallel junction?
cards.explanation: Current splits at a junction; total current equals the sum of branch currents.

cards.front: FORMULA • Equivalent resistance in parallel.
cards.explanation: For parallel resistance, add reciprocals and take the reciprocal to find the equivalent.

cards.front: REASON • Why are household outlets wired in parallel?
cards.explanation: Parallel household branches let individual appliances operate even if another branch opens.

cards.front: ORDER • In a mixed circuit, which network is simplified first?
cards.explanation: Reduce identifiable inner series or parallel groups one at a time in a combination circuit.

cards.front: YES / NO • Does adding a parallel branch increase total resistance?
cards.explanation: Adding a parallel resistance branch increases total conductance, decreasing equivalent resistance.

cards.front: COMPONENT • In a circuit diagram, what controls opening the path?
cards.explanation: A switch opens or closes a circuit's conducting path, controlling whether current can flow.
